options: A data type that stores an entire semi-structured value (like a JSON object) in a single column, with no predefined schema
A special kind of index used only for numeric columns
A Snowflake-specific version of the VARCHAR type with a longer length limit
A stored procedure language for writing loops
questions.explain: VARIANT lets Snowflake store an entire JSON document — whatever shape it is — in one column, without deciding the schema ahead of time.

questions.q: What does the `strip_outer_array = true` file format option do when loading JSON?
options: Loads each element of a top-level JSON array as its own row, instead of loading the whole array as one row
Deletes all array fields from the JSON before loading
Converts JSON arrays into comma-separated strings
Removes the outermost object's keys and keeps only values
questions.explain: Without it, a JSON file that's one big array would load as a single row containing the whole array. strip_outer_array splits it into one row per array element.

questions.q: How does Snowflake actually store data loaded into a VARIANT column?
options: In an optimized internal columnar binary format, not as raw text
As plain uncompressed text, identical to the source file
It doesn't store it — VARIANT columns are computed on the fly from the stage
As a BLOB with no internal structure at all
questions.explain: Snowflake parses and stores VARIANT data in an optimized binary format internally, which is what makes querying into it fast.

questions.q: What does 'schema-on-read' mean in the context of VARIANT, as described in this lesson?
options: You decide the structure of the data when you query it, rather than being forced to define that structure before loading it
Snowflake automatically converts JSON into a relational schema the moment it's loaded
You must write a formal schema file before any COPY INTO will run
It refers to reading data faster than writing it
questions.explain: VARIANT accepts whatever shape the JSON is in at load time; you choose how to interpret and query that structure afterward.

questions.q: Why is loading JSON into a rigid, predefined set of relational columns risky, according to this lesson?
options: If the source JSON adds or changes a field later, a load pipeline built around fixed columns can break
Relational columns can never store numbers from JSON
It's not risky — it's actually the recommended Snowflake approach
JSON files can only be loaded into VARIANT columns, never CSV-style columns
questions.explain: Flattening into fixed columns at load time means the pipeline is brittle to any change in the source JSON's shape — exactly what VARIANT avoids.
